title: The Lagrangian Method for Cooperative Relays & Game Theory in CPS — Derivation, KKT and Worked Example
description: Exam revision of how the Lagrangian method is derived and applied to cooperative relays in CPS: objective, constraints in standard form, building the Lagrangian, why the constraint term is subtracted, the four KKT conditions, the worked example maximize 10p - p^2 subject to 0 <= p <= 3, the shadow price meaning of lambda, the CPS relay utility, the full relay-power Lagrangian with multipliers, stationarity, the log2 quality model, and how the Lagrangian links to cooperative and non-cooperative games.

scenes.title: Why the Lagrangian?
lines: A relay wants more power for better quality, but its battery and the shared budget say no. How do we find the best choice inside the limits?
The Lagrangian method. It combines three things: the objective, which is what the system maximizes; the constraints, which are the limits; and the Lagrangian, which combines both.
We will derive it step by step on a small example, then apply it to cooperative relays in CPS, and link it to game theory.

scenes.title: 1. Start with a constrained problem
lines: Step one: start with a constrained optimization problem. The Lagrangian is built from the objective and the constraints.
The CPS objective: choose relay power p to improve useful transmission performance while accounting for costs.
The constraint: power must stay feasible, between zero and three. The upper limit may represent a battery, hardware, or interference cap.
The example problem: maximize f(p) equals 10p minus p², subject to p minus three at most zero, and p at least zero.
Here p is a simplified, normalized relay power, not a calibrated radio model.

scenes.title: 2. Write inequalities in standard form
lines: Step two: write every inequality in a consistent form. For maximization, these slides write each one as g_i of x at most zero.
General problem: maximize f of x, subject to g_i of x at most zero.
For the example: f(p) equals 10p minus p², and g(p) equals p minus three, at most zero.
Why this form? It lets us attach one non negative multiplier lambda to each constraint, and identify which limits are active at the optimum.
The lower bound p at least zero is also a constraint, but here the optimum will not be at zero.

scenes.title: 3. Build the Lagrangian
lines: Step three: build the Lagrangian. Add the objective, and a multiplier weighted term for each constraint.
General form for maximization: L of x and lambda equals f of x, minus the sum of lambda_i times g_i of x, with every lambda_i at least zero.
Each lambda_i is a Lagrange multiplier.
For our example: L equals 10p minus p², minus lambda times p minus three.
Expanded: L equals 10p minus p², minus lambda p, plus three lambda.
Intuition: the multiplier term makes the constraint part of the calculation. Lambda measures the marginal value of relaxing a binding limit.

scenes.title: 4. Why is the term subtracted?
lines: Step four: why subtract the constraint term? The sign depends on the convention, so stay consistent.
The constraint is g(p) equals p minus three, at most zero. If p exceeds three, it is violated, and p minus three becomes positive.
The term minus lambda times p minus three, with lambda at least zero, then reduces L, like a penalty. A positive lambda makes the upper bound affect the optimum.
So for maximization with g_i at most zero, use L equals f minus the sum of lambda_i g_i. Other textbooks may use different signs, by writing the constraints differently.

scenes.title: 5. The KKT conditions
lines: Step five: derive the KKT conditions. They describe candidate optimal points, under suitable regularity assumptions. There are four.
One, stationarity: the derivative of L with respect to p is 10 minus 2p minus lambda, set equal to zero.
Two, primal feasibility: p minus three at most zero, and p at least zero.
Three, dual feasibility: lambda at least zero.
Four, complementary slackness: lambda times p minus three equals zero.
In words: the solution obeys the limits, multipliers are non negative, and a constraint can have a positive multiplier only when it is active.

scenes.title: 6. Solve the example step by step
lines: Step six: solve the example.
Step A: ignore the constraint for now. Set f prime of p equals 10 minus 2p equal to zero, so p equals 5.
Step B: check feasibility. p equals 5 violates p at most 3. So the maximum feasible point is at the boundary: p star equals 3.
Step C: find the multiplier from stationarity. 10 minus 2 times 3, minus lambda, equals zero. 10 minus 6 is 4, so lambda star equals 4.
Check complementary slackness: lambda is 4, and p minus 3 is zero, so their product is zero. Good.
Step D: compute the objective. f(3) equals 10 times 3, minus 3 squared, which is 30 minus 9, equals 21.

scenes.title: 7. What λ tells us: the shadow price
lines: Step seven: what does the multiplier tell us?
The optimal decision is p star equals 3, the maximum utility is 21, and lambda star equals 4. The upper bound is active.
Lambda is often called a shadow price.
Locally, raising the power cap from 3 to 3 plus epsilon increases the optimal utility by about 4 epsilon, as long as the same active constraint regime holds.
Check it: f of 3.1 is 31 minus 9.61, which is 21.39. That is about 0.4 more, which is 4 times 0.1.
That is the economic meaning of a Lagrange multiplier: the marginal value of relaxing a constraint.

scenes.title: Cooperative relays in CPS: the scenario
lines: Now apply it to real cooperative relaying in CPS.
The goal: choose relay transmit powers to balance communication quality, energy use, and delay, while satisfying system constraints.
The application: industrial sensors send data to a CPS controller through cooperative relays, when the direct wireless link is weak.
A source sensor S forwards data through relay R1 with power p1, and relay R2 with power p2, to the CPS controller that processes the data.

scenes.title: Define the objective
lines: Define the objective: a weighted utility that trades off performance measures.
Maximize U of p1 and p2 equals alpha Q, minus beta E, minus delta D.
Q is communication quality, or reliability. E is energy consumed. D is end to end delay.
Alpha, beta and delta are non negative weights. Increase alpha to prioritize reliability. Increase beta to prioritize energy saving.

scenes.title: Constraints and standard form
lines: Add the system constraints.
Total relay power: p1 plus p2 at most Pmax, the shared power budget.
Individual limits: each p_i between zero and Pimax.
Minimum quality: Q at least Qmin, the minimum acceptable quality.
Now write them in standard form. This deck uses non negative slack expressions:
g1 equals Pmax minus p1 minus p2, at least zero. g2 equals Q minus Qmin, at least zero. g3 equals Pimax minus p_i, at least zero. g4 equals p_i, at least zero.
Each constraint gets a Lagrange multiplier, representing its influence on the optimum.

scenes.title: Construct the relay Lagrangian
lines: Construct the Lagrangian.
L equals alpha Q minus beta E minus delta D,
plus lambda times Pmax minus p1 minus p2,
plus mu times Q minus Qmin,
plus the sum of eta_i times Pimax minus p_i, plus the sum of rho_i times p_i.
Lambda is for the shared power budget, mu for the quality threshold, eta_i for each relay's upper power limit, and rho_i for non negativity. All are at least zero.
Notice the plus signs here: the constraints are written as slack terms that are at least zero. Same idea, different convention, exactly as warned before.

scenes.title: Stationarity and KKT for the relays
lines: Differentiate with respect to each relay power. Set the derivative of L with respect to p_i to zero, for i equals one and two.
Zero equals alpha dQ by dp_i, minus beta dE by dp_i, minus delta dD by dp_i, minus lambda, plus mu dQ by dp_i, minus eta_i, plus rho_i.
Meaning: the marginal quality benefit is balanced against the marginal energy and delay cost, and the active constraints.
Then apply KKT. Stationarity. Primal feasibility, all original constraints hold. Dual feasibility, all multipliers at least zero.
And complementary slackness: lambda times Pmax minus p1 minus p2 equals zero, and mu times Q minus Qmin equals zero.
An inactive constraint has a zero multiplier. An active constraint may have a positive one.

scenes.title: An illustrative quality model
lines: An illustrative quality model, to show how derivatives are calculated.
Q equals log2 of one plus gamma0 plus a1 p1 plus a2 p2.
Assume energy E equals e1 p1 plus e2 p2, and ignore delay.
Then dQ by dp_i equals a_i, divided by ln 2 times one plus gamma0 plus a1 p1 plus a2 p2.
And dE by dp_i equals e_i.
Substitute these into stationarity, and solve jointly with the KKT conditions.

scenes.title: How to solve the model
lines: The practical workflow has five steps.
One, specify Q, E and D using the wireless system model. Two, define the power limits and the quality threshold.
Three, construct L and calculate derivatives. Four, solve stationarity, feasibility, and complementary slackness equations.
Five, check the solution against every constraint.
Real decode and forward systems may also need source to relay and relay to destination constraints, interference, and half duplex factors.

scenes.title: Link to game theory
lines: Finally, the link to game theory. The Lagrangian is an optimization tool, not a type of game.
In a cooperative game, relays coordinate or form a coalition, and optimize a shared system utility, U of A comma P, over the relay set A and power vector P.
The Lagrangian solves this joint constrained resource allocation. The game solution is a coalition choice, with a possible payoff allocation.
In a non cooperative game, each relay chooses its own power to maximize its individual utility, U_i of P_i given the others' powers.
The Lagrangian can solve each player's constrained problem, and best response analysis finds a Nash equilibrium, a best response fixed point.
The general CPS utility adds constraints: P_i between its min and max, D at most Dmax, E at most Emax, and Q at least Qmin.
A caution: KKT conditions are sufficient for a global optimum when the problem is convex. For non convex radio models, KKT may only find local candidates.
Key idea: game theory models strategic interaction, and the Lagrangian handles constrained optimization.

scenes.title: Summary: derivation in five steps
lines: Summary: the derivation in five steps.
One, define the objective: maximize reliability benefit minus energy and delay costs.
Two, write the constraints, converting inequalities to g_i at most zero.
Three, build L equals f minus the sum of lambda_i g_i, with lambda_i at least zero.
Four, apply KKT: stationarity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility, complementary slackness.
Five, solve and interpret. Use lambda as the value of relaxing a constraint. In the example, p star 3, f 21, lambda 4.
Good luck in your exam!
